title: Threshold Oscillation Incident follow-up and SLO rebuild
summary: Post-incident sync to review a threshold oscillation that caused transient throttling and SLO breaches. Discussed root causes (batching + aggressive autoscaler + KV cache cold starts), mitigations (short-term throttling guard, ramped rollout, synthetic canaries), and next steps including logs handoff, SLO rebuild plan, and security signoff for private pilot.
next_steps: Redwood to share filtered throttle logs and sampling scripts by 2026-11-02
Meridian SRE to run provided synthetic canary and feedback by 2026-11-05
Schedule 90-minute bench run for prefix-cache workload with Redwood SE (target week of 2026-11-08)
Redwood to provide updated SLO proposal and rollout playbook by 2026-11-04
Security to complete KMS/SSO checklist review; Redwood and Meridian to confirm encryption at rest details by 2026-11-10
action_items: Diego Ramos - extract throttling traces + top 10 request patterns and upload to shared folder - due 2026-11-02
Liam O'Connor - run synthetic canary with sample prompt set (links in the doc) and share latency histograms - due 2026-11-05
Avery Collins - prepare SLO rebuild doc and mitigation runbook (canary steps, rollback criteria) - due 2026-11-04
Sandra Kim - circulate Meridian security questions spreadsheet and mark items needing deeper review - due 2026-11-03
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-31 11:00 AM PT / 16:00Z — Duration: ~62m. Attendees: Avery Collins (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Nadia Tran (Redwood CSM), Priya Patel (Meridian VP Eng), Liam O'Connor (Meridian SRE), Sandra Kim (Meridian Security), Evan Ross (Meridian PM).

[00:00] Avery Collins: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick us off real quick. we wanted to follow up on the threshold oscillation that you saw last week and make sure we have a concrete mitigation and a plan to rebuild your SLOs.

[00:18] Priya Patel: thanks, avery. i think the team wants clarity on what exactly triggered the oscillation — it looked like we had a steady baseline then a series of spikes and then throttles that fed back into each other.

[00:30] Diego Ramos: yeah, from what we traced the immediate symptom was aggressive request throttling at the routing layer once queue lengths passed the 'hot-path' threshold. but digging in, it's multi-factor: (1) sudden batch size growth due to a few long-sequence requests, (2) autoscaler step that terminated some warm workers during the traffic tail, and (3) a cold prefix/KV cache miss on a subset of model variants which amplified latencies.

[01:02] Liam O'Connor: so two questions — autoscaler triggered scale-in during a load tail? that seems off, we had a scale policy to avoid that. could be our config or how the stepper interprets cpu/gpu utilization.

[01:20] Diego Ramos: correct, the autoscaler used our default 'scale to 0' policy for the burst pools; when a few short bursts finished it stepped aggressively. we recommended smoothing window earlier but it wasn't enabled on that dedicated pool. also, the routing tier applied a threshold-based fallback which started returning 429s and then client-side retry logic increased fanout.

[01:45] Priya Patel: ugh, retries. of course. our SDK default retries are quite chatty. we have a ticket to tune that, but ideally the platform should have a softer failure mode.

[02:02] Avery Collins: absolutely — that's one of the mitigation levers we proposed. for short term we can flip on a "soft-throttle" guard which converts hard 429s to queued slow-path responses for a small percentage of requests, buying time for the autoscaler to stabilize. it's an opt-in toggle for Dedicated customers but we can enable it for your pilot.

[02:20] Evan Ross: can you explain the slow-path responses? will that change cost?

[02:28] Diego Ramos: slow-path will accept the request into a low-priority queue and process with higher batching thresholds but with longer tail latency; it avoids immediate failures which trigger retries. cost might increase a bit because of longer runtime, but it's better than cascading retries and SLO violations. it's a tradeoff — cheaper than full overprovisioning.

[02:56] Sandra Kim: on security, we need to confirm any change to routing behavior doesn't affect our data paths or logging. for compliance we log full request+response IDs and need to ensure retention and access controls remain intact.

[03:12] Avery Collins: understood, sandra. we won't change logging semantics. i'll have Nadia attach the audit log snippet and retention policy we use; also note that this soft-throttle does not touch payloads or KMS keys, it's purely routing logic.

[03:35] Liam O'Connor: you mentioned prefix cache misses earlier — what's the concrete mitigation there?

[03:44] Diego Ramos: two parts: (1) increase baseline warm pool for model variants serving long-sequence workloads; (2) populate warm prefix fragments via a warmup job during scaling events. the problem was that our KV cache entries are per-variant and TTL is short; with scale-in we lost warm state, causing many requests to incur full attention compute.

[04:10] Priya Patel: can we pin the variant to a pool to avoid eviction? we've considered pinning in the past but worried about cost.

[04:20] Diego Ramos: yes you can pin; it's a config toggle for Dedicated. we'd propose a mixed strategy: pin the two heaviest variants and use warmed prefetch for the rest. that limits cost while reducing cold-start latency.

[04:38] Evan Ross: are there known workload patterns that cause the most trouble? for instance, long-context multi-turn chats vs single long prompts?

[04:48] Diego Ramos: multi-turn chats with divergent prefixes — when clients send many unique conversation prefixes — degrade cache hit ratio fastest. single very long prompts also cause big batches and blow up memory pressure. we'll attach the top request signatures we saw.

[05:05] Priya Patel: aside from the immediate fixes, we need a reworked SLO set. our production SLOs were breached during the event and the on-call rotation got paged.

[05:16] Avery Collins: agreed. recommendation is to separate SLOs into fast-path P50/P90 with a small fast-path SLO and a distinct long-tail SLO that accounts for slow-path processing. also add a "sustained-load" guard to trigger canary scaling early — basically conservative early scaling.

[05:40] Liam O'Connor: will that change our alerts? we want fewer pagers for transient spikes but still get notified on sustained degradation.

[05:49] Nadia Tran: yes, the new alerting proposal uses a duration window (e.g., 5m for page, 30m for SLT) and suppresses pages if we see the soft-throttle active with expected backlog. we'll include the exact thresholds in the SLO doc.

[06:06] Sandra Kim: about compliance again — we're evaluating whether the fallback policy or queued slow-path affects our data residency constraints since queued requests might be routed to other regions in fallback. that's a blocker unless we limit fallback to same-region variants.

[06:22] Diego Ramos: good point. we have region affinity toggles. for privacy-sensitive tenants we can disable cross-region fallback and only use same-region slow-path. that will be part of the rollout playbook.

[06:40] Priya Patel: what's the proposed timeline for implementing these mitigations? we need to present to execs a remediation plan by next week.

[06:49] Avery Collins: short-term (48–72h): provide throttle traces, enable soft-throttle toggle in your environment (canary 5% traffic), and share SLO rebuild draft. medium-term (1–2 weeks): run synthetic canaries, pin selected variants, and deploy warmup jobs. long-term (2–6 weeks): refine autoscaler smoothing, add sustained-load canary, and verify with an in-situ bench.

[07:20] Evan Ross: okay. can you run the bench on our dataset? we have a representative prompt corpus but can't run at full scale yet.

[07:30] Diego Ramos: yes, we'll coordinate a 90-minute bench with your SREs. we need sample prompts and a whitelist of model variants; we'll simulate realistic retry behavior. we'll also run with kv-cache instrumentation turned on so you can see hit rates.

[07:52] Priya Patel: excellent. one more thing — during the incident we saw odd error strings in the logs where 'K/V' was transcribed as 'kay vee' in a few alerts; small thing but makes debugging annoying. can you standardize the logging names?

[08:05] Diego Ramos: noted — we'll normalize metric names (kv_cache_hit -> KV_CACHE_HIT) in the next patch.

[08:14] Sandra Kim: security also wants to confirm KMS key rotation timelines and whether the warmup job touches plaintext. we need an explicit statement that warmup prefetches only model prefixes and never persists payloads unencrypted outside the ram.

[08:30] Avery Collins: confirmed: warmup prefetch is in-memory only, uses customer-managed KMS for any persisted artifacts, and we will provide a short security brief that Nadia will attach.

[08:45] Liam O'Connor: for the canary, what are rollback criteria? we need strict thresholds so we can flip back quickly if things regress.

[08:54] Diego Ramos: rollback criteria proposal: if fast-path P95 increases by >15% relative to baseline or error rates exceed 0.5% for more than 3 consecutive minutes, rollback. we'll put exact numbers in the runbook; these are starting points.

[09:12] Priya Patel: sounds reasonable. also, we'll want to see cost delta estimates so we can approve pinning variants.

[09:21] Avery Collins: we'll include cost delta tables: pinning two variants, enabling soft-throttle, warmup job CPU/GPU costs. quick estimate now is <8% change for pin+warmup on your current commit. we'll produce exact numbers after we analyze your recent traffic (Diego's action).

[09:40] Evan Ross: any potential vendor lock-in concerns if we enable these platform toggles? CFO asked about exit paths.

[09:49] Avery Collins: key point: all of these are config toggles; you can roll back to default behavior anytime. for Dedicated/Private setups we provide exportable audit logs and a migration checklist. nothing here forces a proprietary data format.

[10:08] Nadia Tran: i'll attach links after the call: SLO template, playbook template, and the security checklist.

[10:15] Priya Patel: great. can we summarize next steps and owners?

[10:20] Avery Collins: quick recap — Diego shares throttle traces + top signatures (due 11/02). Avery will draft SLO rebuild and runbook (due 11/04). Liam runs synthetic canary and shares results (due 11/05). Sandra to mark security follow-ups (due 11/03). Redwood to schedule bench with your SRE for week of 11/08.

[10:40] Priya Patel: that matches our expectations. thanks everyone — let's keep communication tight, we need to close the remediation before next release.

[10:52] Avery Collins: thanks folks. we'll follow up in email with links and calendar invites.

End of transcript. Some transcription artifacts: speaker turn labels occasionally misattributed; timestamps approximate.
